plan.factor: Framework T-atom ratio of the gel: Si relative to the trivalent/other framework-forming heteroatoms Al and P, i.e. Si/(Al + P + small constant)
queries: gel Si/Al ratio effect on zeolite framework type MFI FAU CHA
Si/Al ratio aluminophosphate SAPO AFI CHA synthesis gel composition
plan.why: Tree ensembles can only threshold single columns, and every gel input is a normalized mole fraction, so the crucial compositional regime - whether the batch is a pure-silica or high-Si system (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW), an aluminosilicate with moderate Si/Al (FAU, LTA, MOR, CHA), or an aluminophosphate / SAPO-type batch dominated by P and Al (AFI, AEL, AEI, LEV) - emerges only from the ratio of Si to Al+P and is not directly available. Literature syntheses transfer poorly across papers largely because a fixed Al (or P) mole fraction means different things at different Si levels; encoding the T-atom ratio as a single split-able column lets the held-out-publication model separate these three chemical regimes immediately, which none of the D0 columns can do alone.

descriptor.assumptions: (1) Al and P are the only significant framework heteroatoms at the level of a first descriptor; other framework-forming atoms present in the data (B, Ga, Ge, Zn, Be, Ti, Sn, Zr, V, Fe-type) are rarer and are deliberately excluded to keep the descriptor simple and general, which misclassifies their regime slightly (e.g., a borosilicate batch reads as high Si/(Al+P) even though B is a framework T-atom). (2) All gel Al and P are assumed to be framework-incorporable, ignoring speciation (e.g., extra P as mineralizer or Al in the liquid phase), which is only approximately true. (3) The additive constant 0.001 is negligible for any real gel (Al+P > 0.001 in mole fraction for essentially all literature recipes) and only prevents division by zero for pure-silica batches; it maps those to very large values, which is the intended regime. (4) The ratio is a regime indicator, not a mechanistic quantity; it does not capture OSDA-specific or cation-specific structure direction, which subsequent rounds must cover.
descriptor.expected_effect: As Si/(Al+P) increases from ~0: first AlPO/SAPO-type frameworks (AFI, AEL, AEI, LEV, AEN) dominate; at intermediate values (roughly 1-100 depending on cations/OSDA) aluminosilicates (FAU, LTA, MOR, CHA, FER, TON) are favored; at very large values pure-silica frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, MEL) and Failed pure-silica entries dominate. Failed is also expected at the extreme tails of each regime when the ratio is mismatched with the OSDA/cation set.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out-publication accuracy does not improve (or degrades) when this column is added, and feature-importance analysis shows the new column receiving negligible split importance, then the ratio adds no information beyond the individual mole fractions - i.e., the trees were already resolving the regime from absolute Si, Al, P levels and their interactions, contradicting the hypothesis. A second falsifier: if frameworks known to be insensitive to Si/Al (e.g., purely fluoride-mediated pure-silica phases) show systematic misclassification driven by the new column.
descriptor.hypothesis: The Si/(Al+P) gel ratio is the primary compositional variable that separates the three major synthesis regimes in zeolite chemistry: pure-silica/high-Si batches (large Si/(Al+P)) crystallize purely siliceous frameworks such as MFI, *BEA, MTW, MEL and MWW; intermediate ratios yield aluminosilicates whose topology is set by the Si/Al balance together with the inorganic cation and OSDA (FAU, LTA, MOR, CHA, FER, TON); and low ratios dominated by Al and P correspond to aluminophosphate/SAPO chemistry that gives AFI, AEL, AEI, LEV, AEN. Because every D0 composition input is a normalized mole fraction summing to 1, a RandomForest can only see absolute Si, Al and P levels, not their ratio, so the model currently cannot place a recipe in the correct regime with a single split. Adding Si/(Al+P+0.001) as one column gives the trees immediate access to this regime variable.
descriptor.mechanism: Framework T-atom speciation is governed by gel stoichiometry: framework Al and P each require charge-balancing species (Na+, K+, OSDA+, or paired Al-O-P in SAPOs), and the amount of heteroatom relative to Si controls the population of building units (e.g., D6Rs and 6MRs favored at low Si/Al in FAU/LTA/CHA, vs. all-silica pentasil chains and 5-1 units at high Si/Si+Al). At very high Si/(Al+P) the gel lacks charge-balancing demand and cation/OSDA effects dominate, favoring pure-silica phases; at intermediate values the Al level sets how much cation is sequestered, shifting between dense-to-open aluminosilicate frameworks; near zero, P and Al are abundant and AlPO4-type lattices (AFI, AEL, AEI, LEV) form with F- or OH-mineralizer control. Tree ensembles can exploit a threshold on the ratio directly, whereas they cannot reproduce a ratio by splitting on normalized mole fractions alone. Literature syntheses consistently report that small changes in Si/Al change the product framework (e.g., gel Si/Al=30 gives MFI plus impurity while 40-80 gives the target aluminosilicate phase [5]; Si/Al > 50 shifts MCM-22-type systems away from competing MFI/MTW coprecipitation [4]; interzeolite CHA crystallization tracks the Si/Al of the starting FAU over Si/Al ~ 14-93 [1], [2], [6]).
descriptor.name: gel_Si_over_trivalent_ratio

plan.factor: Gel alkalinity: mineralizer strength OH per framework-forming T atom
queries: effect of gel alkalinity OH/SiO2 ratio on zeolite framework selectivity MFI FAU MOR
fluoride medium low alkalinity synthesis high silica zeolites versus hydroxide route
plan.why: After the Si/(Al+P) ratio places a recipe in the pure-silica, aluminosilicate, or aluminophosphate regime, the next dominant lever in zeolite synthesis is alkalinity. The hydroxide-to-framework-former ratio controls gel dissolution and crystallization rate, the mineralizing regime (near-neutral fluoride route vs strongly basic NaOH route), and hence framework selectivity: low-alkalinity fluoride media favor high-silica, low-framework-density phases (MTW, MFI, *BEA, STT-type phases) while high OH/(Si+Al+P) pushes toward low-Si, dense or open aluminosilicates (FAU, LTA, MOR) and fast OSA/Failed outcomes at extremes. Because every D0 composition column is a normalized mole fraction summing to 1, a tree can split on absolute OH but cannot express it relative to the Si, Al and P available to dissolve; OH/(Si+Al+P+0.001) is a genuinely new joint quantity that one column at a time the model cannot access.

descriptor.assumptions: OH mole fraction is taken as the total mineralizer strength, but in fluoride syntheses F- acts as an alternative mineralizer and is not credited here; the OH column may not capture Na2O/K2O contributions to basicity in records where only salts are listed; OSDA hydroxide salts contribute to the OH column implicitly, conflating template dose with alkalinity; contributions of B, Ga, Ge, Ti etc. to framework-forming T atoms are ignored (only Si+Al+P counted).
descriptor.expected_effect: As OH/(Si+Al+P) increases: purely siliceous frameworks (MFI, MTW, *BEA, MEL, Si-CHA) and Failed outcomes should give way to aluminosilicates (FAU, LTA, MOR, CHA) and then to dense/impurity phases and Failed at the highest alkalinities, particularly for Na-rich gels.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out publications show that recipes with similar Si/(Al+P) and cation content yield the same framework across a wide range of OH/(Si+Al+P), while the descriptor fails to reduce confusion between e.g. MFI and FAU or between CHA and dense phases, the alkalinity hypothesis is contradicted for this dataset. Also, if fluoride-route batches (F > 0) with very low OH/T behave like high-alkalinity batches, the descriptor's low-end interpretation is wrong.
descriptor.hypothesis: After the Si/(Al+P) ratio assigns a recipe to the pure-silica, aluminosilicate, or aluminophosphate regime, gel alkalinity per framework-forming T atom is the next dominant lever on framework selectivity. Low OH/T (often fluoride-mediated, near-neutral batches) favors high-silica, low-framework-density phases such as MFI, MTW, *BEA, MEL and Si-CHA; intermediate-to-high OH/T drives conventional aluminosilicate crystallization (FAU, LTA, MOR, CHA, FER, TON); very high OH/T destabilizes gels and pushes toward dense phases (ANA-type, GIS-type), cation-bearing impurity phases, or Failed/amorphous outcomes.
descriptor.mechanism: Hydroxide is the mineralizing agent under basic conditions: it catalyzes polymerization–depolymerization of silicate and aluminate species, so the OH/T ratio sets the dissolution rate of the amorphous gel, the equilibrium silicate speciation (Qn distribution), and the nucleation rate. High OH/T accelerates dissolution and nucleation, promotes incorporation of the charge-compensating inorganic cations, and shifts selectivity toward Al-dense, cation-rich frameworks; insufficient OH/T leaves the gel under-mineralized (Failed) unless fluoride provides the mineralizing role in acidic media, where slower dissolution favors defect-poor high-silica frameworks. Because every D0 composition column is a normalized mole fraction summing to 1, a tree can only split on absolute OH and cannot express it relative to the T atoms available to dissolve, so OH/(Si+Al+P) is a genuinely new joint quantity.

plan.factor: gel dilution: water content per framework-forming T atom, H2O / (Si + Al + P)
queries: effect of water content gel dilution zeolite synthesis framework density phase selectivity
water to silica ratio crystallization FAU CHA dense phase impurity
plan.why: After the Si/(Al+P) ratio sets the compositional regime and OH/(Si+Al+P) sets the alkalinity, the remaining dominant lever in the gel is dilution. Because all composition inputs are normalized mole fractions summing to 1, H2O in D0 is a small absolute number (typically 0.5-0.9) whose meaning depends on how much framework former is present: a concentrated gel with H2O/T of a few units crystallizes fast toward dense or metastable phases (ANA, GIS, sodalite, or Failed), while dilute gels with H2O/T of tens to hundreds slow nucleation and favor open, low-framework-density phases (FAU, CHA, *BEA, AFI, AEL) and allow large OSDA-templated pores. Tree ensembles see H2O and T atoms only as separate absolute columns, so the ratio is invisible to the current model. This descriptor is also publication-portable since it is a dimensionless batch ratio, not an absolute recipe scale.

descriptor.assumptions: Assumes (1) the reported gel water mole fraction reflects the true crystallization-medium water content (no evaporation, dry-gel conversion, vapor-phase transport, or solvent-free protocols, which this descriptor cannot represent); (2) Si+Al+P is an adequate proxy for total framework-forming T atoms, ignoring Ge, B, Ti, Ga, Zn and other heteroatom formers present in small amounts; (3) the phase-density trend documented mainly for pure-silica fluoride and hydroxide syntheses transfers to aluminosilicate and aluminophosphate systems, where Al or F charge compensation may be absent and the trend may weaken; (4) 0.001 guards against division by zero in essentially water-free or T-free records but such recipes (e.g., solvent-free syntheses) fall outside the descriptor's intended domain.
descriptor.expected_effect: As the descriptor increases (more dilute gel), predicted products should shift toward higher-framework-density phases (e.g., from *BEA/MWW/CHA toward MFI, MTW, dense or Failed outcomes) because effective OSDA concentration per T atom falls. As the descriptor decreases (concentrated gel), low-framework-density, large-cage phases such as *BEA, MWW, CHA and cage-rich fluoride phases should become more likely. Note this is the opposite sign of the intuitive 'dilution favors open frameworks' expectation and follows the experimentally documented trend for OSDA-mediated silica syntheses.
descriptor.falsification: If held-out publications show no systematic association between H2O/(Si+Al+P) and framework density of the product after controlling for Si/(Al+P) and OH/T — for example, if dense phases are equally frequent in concentrated and dilute gels, or if open low-FD phases dominate at high dilution — the hypothesis is contradicted. A specific contradiction of the cited trend would be observing that lowering H2O/T (raising concentration) consistently yields denser rather than less dense products in OSDA-mediated syntheses.
descriptor.hypothesis: The water-to-framework-former ratio (H2O/T, where T = Si+Al+P) is a phase-selectivity lever independent of the already-provided regime (Si/(Al+P)) and alkalinity (OH/(Si+Al+P)) descriptors. Because all gel species are normalized mole fractions summing to 1, H2O in D0 is a small absolute number whose meaning depends entirely on how much framework former is present; a tree ensemble can only split on absolute H2O, so it cannot see this dimensionless dilution ratio. Low H2O/T (concentrated gels) raises the effective concentrations of all dissolved species relative to water, most importantly the OSDA cation, and is experimentally observed to steer crystallization toward open, low-framework-density phases with high organic content (e.g., *BEA, MWW, CHA, clathrate-cage phases, large-pore fluoride phases). High H2O/T (dilute gels) lowers supersaturation and the effective OSDA/T ratio, slowing nucleation and favoring denser phases or, at extremes, Failed/amorphous outcomes or slow transformations to denser impurity phases.
descriptor.mechanism: Decreasing H2O/SiO2 at fixed molar recipe increases the concentration of the organic SDA in the liquid phase of the crystallizing mixture; open frameworks with larger pore/cage volume must occlude more SDA per framework T atom, so they pay a greater energetic penalty unless the SDA (and charge-compensating F- or Al) is sufficiently concentrated. Hence concentrated gels favor low-framework-density, high-organic-content phases, while dilution shifts selectivity toward denser frameworks. Dilution also changes F- concentration in fluoride media, reinforcing the same trend since F- is occluded and stabilizes open frameworks. Additionally, water activity governs hydrolysis/condensation kinetics: dilute gels slow nucleation, giving more time for Ostwald-competitive transformations toward thermodynamically denser products.
